match.reason: The closest bank point, the bill of rights debate, covers only the argument over a national bill of rights and who should protect rights, whereas the new point teaches three routes to reform (new laws, a charter, or the courts), so it is related but not the same idea.

note:
A fresh check found these problems in this version. Fix each one, and keep everything that is right:
- Question b, wording: The why says a charter was not involved, but the question never says so. In Victoria, judges often read unclear laws to protect rights because the Charter (s 32) tells them to, so 'Reform through a charter of rights' is a tempting option. Add a phrase such as 'without relying on a charter' to the question to remove the doubt.

rejected.title: Reforming rights protection
card: Reform means a change to make a right better protected. In Australia, reform can come through parliament, a charter of rights or the courts.
New laws
parliament can pass a new Act or change an old one. For example, an anti-discrimination Act can give people a way to complain when their rights are not respected.
Charter of rights
a law that lists certain rights and says how governments and public bodies must treat them. Victoria has one, the Charter of Human Rights and Responsibilities Act 2006.
Courts
when judges decide a case, they may interpret a law in a way that protects a right. This can change how the law is applied in later cases.
rejected.remember: Rights protection can be reformed by parliament, by a charter, or by court decisions.

a.q: What does a charter of rights do?
opts: Lists rights and how public bodies must treat them
Records how judges read unclear laws in past cases
Protects one right, such as freedom from discrimination
Sets rules for private businesses, not governments
a.why: A charter is a law that lists a set of rights and says how governments and public bodies must treat them. Recording how judges read laws describes reform through the courts, not a charter. A charter also covers many rights, not just one.
a.clue: Think about who a charter tells how to act.

b.q: A judge hears a case and reads an unclear law so that it protects a person's right. Other judges then follow this reading in later cases. What kind of reform is this?
opts: Reform through the courts
Reform through a new Act of parliament
Reform through a charter of rights
Reform through a change of government
b.why: The change came from a judge interpreting a law in a case, and it then shaped later cases. Parliament did not pass anything new, so it is not a new law. A charter was not involved, so that option is also wrong.
b.clue: Who made the change, and in what setting?

a.q: Parliament passes an Act that gives people a new way to complain about unfair treatment. Which kind of reform is this?
opts: A new law made by parliament
A change made through a court decision
A new charter of rights for the state
A change made by judges interpreting law
a.why: Parliament made a new Act, so the reform came through a new law. It was not a court decision, because no judge decided a case, and it did not create a charter listing rights.
a.clue: Who made the change: parliament or a judge?

b.why: The change came from a judge interpreting a law in a case, and it then shaped later cases. Parliament did not pass anything new, so it is not a new law. A charter was not involved, so that option is also wrong.
b.clue: Who made the change, and in what setting?

a.best: A new law made by parliament

problems.detail: The stem says 'Parliament passes an Act' and the right option repeats 'made by parliament', so a student can match words without knowing the idea. The clue ('parliament or a judge?') makes it even more obvious. Two wrong options ('A change made through a court decision' and 'A change made by judges interpreting law') mean nearly the same thing, so both can be ruled out together. That leaves little real choice.
